client: I've been really struggling lately with this overwhelming anxiety about my final exams coming up next month. After how badly last term went for me, I just can't stop my mind from spiraling into worst-case scenarios about failing again. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I had to try something.
therapist: It takes real courage to reach out even when part of you doubts it will help — that ambivalence makes complete sense given how draining last term was for you. It sounds like your mind is working overtime right now, pulling you toward those "what if I fail again" spirals, and that kind of anticipatory anxiety can feel exhausting even before the exams arrive. I'd love to gently explore those worst-case thoughts with you — can you tell me what the most persistent or frightening one looks like when it shows up?

client: The thought that keeps hitting me hardest is that if I fail these exams, it'll prove that I'm just not smart enough to be here, like last term wasn't a fluke but actually the truth about me. It plays on a loop, especially late at night when I'm trying to study and I can't focus. And the scary part is that the more I try to push it away, the louder it gets.
therapist: That thought — "this is the truth about me" — is such a painful one to carry, and it makes sense it feels loudest in those quiet, vulnerable moments at night when you're already tired and stretched thin. What you're describing is a really common CBT pattern called a "core belief," where one difficult experience gets treated by our mind as permanent evidence about our whole identity, rather than one hard chapter in a longer story. I'm curious — if a close friend came to you with exactly the same situation, struggling after a tough term, would you tell them it proved they didn't belong there?

client: No, of course I wouldn't say that to a friend, I'd probably tell them one bad term doesn't define them and they should keep trying. But when I try to apply that same logic to myself, it just... doesn't land the same way, it feels hollow somehow. Like I know intellectually it's the "right" thing to think, but it doesn't actually make the fear go away.
therapist: What you're noticing is really insightful — there's often a gap between what we *know* logically and what we actually *feel* to be true, and that gap can make good advice feel frustratingly empty when we try to apply it to ourselves. That hollowness is actually a signal that the fear isn't really about logic at all — it's rooted in something deeper, maybe a long-held story about what you need to prove or be in order to belong. I'm wondering, do you have a sense of where that story — "I need to be smart enough to deserve my place here" — might have first come from for you?

client: I think it probably goes back to growing up in a family where academic achievement was kind of everything, like my parents never said outright that love was conditional on grades, but it always felt that way. I remember getting a B once in middle school and my dad just going quiet and disappointed for days, and that silence said more than any words could have. But I'm not sure how digging into all that history actually helps me get through my exams next month, it feels like we're moving away from the problem rather than solving it.
therapist: That memory of your dad's silence is so telling — it shows how deeply and quietly that message got wired in, that your worth was tied to your performance, and it makes complete sense that it still echoes now when exams feel high-stakes. And your pushback is completely fair — the history matters because it's the *root* of why failing an exam doesn't just feel disappointing to you, it feels like an identity threat, which is why the anxiety is so much louder than the situation alone would explain. So with that in mind, I'd love to work on something practical with you — when that loop starts at night, what does the very first thought usually look like before it spirals?

client: Usually it starts with something pretty small, like I'll read a practice question and not immediately know the answer, and then almost instantly my brain jumps to "see, you don't know this, you're going to fail." It escalates really fast from there into the whole spiral about not belonging and everyone finding out I'm not as capable as they think. I guess I never really noticed there was a starting point before it all blurred together, so that's actually kind of interesting to pay attention to.
therapist: It's really meaningful that you just noticed that trigger point — that small moment of uncertainty becoming "proof" of failure — because that's exactly where we can start to intervene before the spiral gains momentum. That jump from "I don't know this answer yet" to "I don't belong here" is what we call a cognitive distortion, specifically a kind of all-or-nothing thinking where a single moment of not-knowing gets treated as total evidence of incompetence. What do you think might actually be a more accurate interpretation of not immediately knowing an answer to a practice question?

client: I guess a more accurate interpretation would be that I'm still learning and that's literally the whole point of doing practice questions, not knowing something yet doesn't mean I'll never know it. But here's my worry, in the moment when that thought hits at like midnight when I'm already exhausted and panicking, I genuinely don't know if I'll be able to stop and think rationally like this. It feels very different to understand this calmly right now in a conversation versus actually catching myself in the middle of a spiral.
therapist: You just came up with that reframe so naturally — "I'm still learning and that's the point" — that's genuinely yours now, not something I handed you, and that matters. You're also being really wise to anticipate the gap between calm insight and midnight panic, which is exactly why in CBT we don't just rely on in-the-moment reasoning — instead we prepare a kind of "anchor" in advance, like a short written phrase you've already chosen for yourself, so exhausted-midnight-you doesn't have to think, just remember. Would you be open to trying to put that reframe into one simple sentence you could keep somewhere visible for those moments?

client: I can try that, maybe something like "not knowing yet is part of learning, it doesn't mean I don't belong here." But I'll be honest, I'm a little skeptical that a sticky note or a phone reminder is going to cut through the kind of panic I get into, it feels almost too simple for how intense the spiral gets. I don't want to dismiss it before trying, but I guess I'm worried I'll look at it and my brain will just go "yeah but this time it's different, this time you really are failing."
therapist: That phrase you came up with is genuinely powerful, and your skepticism about it is actually really healthy — it means you're thinking critically rather than just hoping a quick fix will work. You're right that in intense moments your brain will likely argue back, which is why the note isn't meant to *silence* the spiral but just to create a tiny pause, a moment of friction that gives you a foothold before the avalanche. I'm curious — in the past, even in your worst spirals, has there ever been anything, even something small, that helped you find even a brief moment of ground?

client: Honestly, the one thing that sometimes helps is stepping away from my desk and just making a cup of tea, there's something about the routine of it that briefly interrupts the noise in my head. But I always feel guilty doing it, like I'm wasting time I should be using to study, so even that small relief comes with its own anxiety attached to it. It's kind of exhausting that even my coping mechanisms feel like they're working against me.
therapist: That tea ritual sounds like genuine wisdom your nervous system already discovered — a small, grounding routine that interrupts the spiral — and it's so telling that even that moment of relief gets hijacked by guilt, as though your mind won't allow you any rest without a cost. That guilt is actually the same core belief showing up in a different costume: "I only deserve to be here if I'm constantly grinding," which is exhausting because it leaves no safe ground at all. What do you think would happen to your studying if you gave yourself full permission to take that tea break — do you think it would actually make things worse, or is there another possibility?

client: Honestly, if I'm being rational about it, I'd probably study better after a short break because I'd be less frantic and more able to actually absorb information. But giving myself "full permission" feels almost impossible, like there's this internal voice that would still be judging me the whole time I was making the tea, so I'm not sure the break would even feel like a real break. I think the guilt would just follow me into it and I'd end up rushing back to my desk before I'd actually calmed down at all.
therapist: You already know the rational answer — breaks help you study better — and yet that internal judge follows you even into the moments meant for rest, which sounds genuinely exhausting, like there's no room that feels safe. That critical voice during the break is worth paying attention to, because it's doing the same job as the midnight spiral — keeping you in a state of constant self-surveillance so you never fully land anywhere. I'm wondering, what do you imagine that internal judge is actually trying to protect you from — what does it fear would happen if you truly let yourself rest without guilt?

client: I think the judge is terrified that if I relax even a little, I'll lose my edge and slip into the same complacency that led to last term going badly, like rest equals danger somehow. It's almost like the anxiety and guilt are trying to be helpful in a twisted way, keeping me on high alert so I don't get blindsided by failure again. That's a weird thing to realize, that the thing making me miserable might actually think it's protecting me.
therapist: That's a genuinely profound realization — recognizing that your anxiety isn't your enemy but a misguided protector trying to keep you safe is one of the most important shifts that can happen in this kind of work, and the fact that you arrived there yourself says a lot about your self-awareness. The problem isn't that it wants to protect you, it's that it learned the wrong lesson from last term — that relentless pressure and hypervigilance are what keep failure away, when actually they might be part of what made last term so hard. I'm curious, what do you think actually *did* contribute to last term being difficult — was it really a lack of vigilance, or were there other factors the anxious judge might be overlooking?
